# m05-l02 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

Kinetic Friction.

Kinetic friction is the force exerted on one surface by another when the two surfaces rub because one or both are moving.

Our big question for this lesson: what force causes a train to stop? Let's begin smaller. Push a book across your desk, then stop pushing. The book stops. Why? Friction!

The book felt a kind of friction that acts on moving objects, called kinetic friction. Kinetic friction is the force one surface exerts on another when the two rub against each other because one or both of them are moving. Friction also brings a train to a stop. The brakes rub against the turning wheels, and the grip of the rails on the wheels slows the whole train.

## Slide 2

Static Friction.

Static friction is the force exerted on one surface by another when there is no motion between the two surfaces.

Now try pushing a couch across the floor, like on the left of Figure 10. You push gently, and nothing happens. Newton's laws say the net force on the couch must be zero. So a second horizontal force must be pushing back, equal in size to yours. That's static friction: the force one surface exerts on another when there's no motion between them.

Push harder, and the couch still doesn't budge. Static friction grows to match your push. But there's a limit to how big static friction can get. When you push hard enough to beat that maximum static friction, the couch starts to move, as on the right of Figure 10. From then on, kinetic friction acts on it instead.

## Slide 4

What Affects Friction?

Friction depends on the materials of the surfaces and on the normal force between them.

The materials that surfaces are made of affect friction. There's more friction between your shoes and concrete than between your socks and a polished wood floor.

You might guess that friction also depends on how much surface area is touching, or how fast the surfaces slide past each other. Experiments show that these matter very little. But the normal force between the two objects does matter. The harder one object is pressed against the other, the greater the friction. So the two factors that affect friction are the kinds of surfaces and the normal force.

## Slide 5

Measuring Kinetic Friction.

Kinetic friction force is directly proportional to the normal force.

Imagine pulling a block along a surface at a constant velocity, as in Figure 11. The block isn't accelerating, so by Newton's laws, the friction force must be equal and opposite to your pull. The spring scale shows that force. Stack more blocks on top to raise the normal force, and measure again.

Table 1 shows results for a block on sandpaper. With 1 block, the normal force is 0.98 newtons and kinetic friction is 0.53 newtons. With 2 blocks, 1.96 newtons and 0.95 newtons. With 3 blocks, 2.94 newtons and 1.4 newtons. With 4 blocks, 3.92 newtons and 1.8 newtons. With 5 blocks, 4.90 newtons and 2.3 newtons. With 6 blocks, 5.88 newtons and 3.1 newtons. With 7 blocks, 6.86 newtons and 3.3 newtons. And with 8 blocks, 7.84 newtons and 4.0 newtons. As the normal force goes up, so does the friction.

## Slide 6

The Coefficient of Kinetic Friction.

The kinetic friction force equals the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force: F sub f, kinetic, equals mu sub k times F sub N.

Plot the data, and you get a graph like Figure 12. Kinetic friction and normal force have a linear relationship. Each line on the graph is for a different surface. The sandpaper line is steeper than the line for the highly polished table. That makes sense: pulling a block across sandpaper should be much harder than across a polished table. So the slope tells you how big the friction will be.

That slope is called the coefficient of kinetic friction, written with the Greek letter mu and a subscript k. It relates the friction force to the normal force. Comparing the three lines in Figure 12, sandpaper has the largest coefficient, about 0.5, the rough table is in the middle, and the highly polished table has the smallest.

As an equation: the kinetic friction force equals mu sub k times the normal force. This is why railway maintenance should include cleaning the wheels, not just the tracks. Dirt, oil, or other gunk on the wheels changes the surfaces in contact and lowers the coefficient of friction, so a train can't grip the rails as well when it brakes.

## Slide 7

Static Friction, by the Numbers.

The static friction force is less than or equal to the coefficient of static friction times the normal force.

Maximum static friction relates to the normal force in a similar way. Remember, static friction only acts in response to a force trying to start a resting object moving. If nothing is trying to move the object, static friction is zero. If something is, static friction grows up to a maximum value, and then it's overcome and motion begins.

As an equation: the static friction force is less than or equal to mu sub s times the normal force, where mu sub s is the coefficient of static friction between the two surfaces. The maximum static friction that must be overcome before motion starts is mu sub s times F sub N. For the couch in Figure 10, the maximum static friction exactly balances the person's push the instant before the couch starts to move.

Note that these friction equations involve only the magnitudes of the forces. And friction forces always act perpendicular to the normal force.

## Slide 8

Real-World Physics, Rough Up Close.

All surfaces are rough at the microscopic level, and touching high points temporarily bond.

Every surface, even one that looks perfectly smooth, is rough at the microscopic level. Look at an image of a graphite crystal magnified by a scanning tunneling microscope, and you'll see bumps and dips at the level of atoms.

When two surfaces touch, their high points make contact and temporarily bond. That's where both static and kinetic friction come from. The details of how this works are still unknown, and they're an active area of research in both physics and engineering.

## Slide 9

Coefficients of Friction.

Coefficients of friction are estimates that depend strongly on the condition of the surfaces.

Table 2 lists typical coefficients of friction, static first and then kinetic. Cast iron on cast iron: 1.1 and 0.15. Glass on glass: 0.94 and 0.4. Leather on oak: 0.61 and 0.52. Nonstick coating on steel: 0.04 and 0.04. Oak on oak: 0.62 and 0.48. Steel on steel: 0.78 and 0.42. And steel on steel with castor oil: just 0.15 and 0.08.

These values are estimates for each pair of surfaces. Measurements are very sensitive to surface conditions. Impurities like dust, or tiny amounts of oil from the experimenters' hands, can change the results a lot.

Here's a cause-and-effect puzzle. Systems can be designed to cause a desired effect. Car and airplane makers use steel for many parts. Do you think any steel parts touch each other directly in a vehicle? What would happen if they did? Use the evidence in Table 2 to explain your answer.

## Slide 10

Example Problem 3, Balanced Friction Forces.

At constant velocity, the pushing force equals the kinetic friction force.

You push a 25.0 kilogram wooden box across a wooden floor at a constant speed of 1.0 meter per second. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. How hard are you pushing on the box?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Identify the forces and set up a coordinate system. Draw a motion diagram showing constant v and a equals zero. Draw the free-body diagram. Known: m is 25.0 kilograms, v is 1.0 meter per second, a is 0.0 meters per second squared, and mu sub k is 0.20. Unknown: the force of the person on the box.

Step two: solve. The normal force is in the y-direction, and the box doesn't accelerate that way. So the normal force equals negative F sub g, which is negative m g: negative 25.0 kilograms times negative 9.8 newtons per kilogram, or positive 245 newtons. The push is in the x-direction, and since v is constant the box doesn't accelerate. So the force of the person on the box equals mu sub k times the normal force: 0.20 times 245 newtons, or 49 newtons, to the right.

Step three: evaluate. Force is measured in newtons. The positive sign agrees with the sketch. And the push is one fifth of the box's weight, which matches mu sub k equals 0.20, or one fifth.

## Slide 11

Example Problem 4, Unbalanced Friction Forces.

When the push is greater than friction, a equals the push minus friction, over m.

Now imagine you double the force on the 25.0 kilogram box from Example Problem 3. What is the box's acceleration? And how far will you push it in 3 seconds?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw a motion diagram showing v and a, and a free-body diagram with the doubled push. Known: m is 25.0 kilograms, mu sub k is 0.20, v is 1.0 meter per second, the push is 2 times 49 newtons, or 98 newtons, and t is 3.0 seconds. Unknown: a.

Step two, part one. The normal force is in the y-direction, and there's no acceleration that way, so F sub N equals negative F sub g, or negative m g. But the box does accelerate in the x-direction, so the forces there are unequal. F net equals the push minus friction. Substitute m a for F net, and a equals the push minus friction, over m. Friction equals mu sub k times F sub N, which is mu sub k m g. So a equals 98 newtons minus 0.20 times 25.0 kilograms times 9.8 newtons per kilogram, all over 25.0 kilograms. That's 2.0 meters per second squared.

Part two. Use the relationship between distance, time, and constant acceleration: final position equals initial position plus initial velocity times t, plus one half a t squared. Starting at 0 meters, that's 1.0 meter per second times 3.0 seconds, plus one half times 2.0 meters per second squared times the square of 3.0 seconds. That's 3 meters plus 9 meters, or 12 meters.

Step three: evaluate. Acceleration is in meters per second squared and position is in meters. In this coordinate system, the sign should be positive, and it is. And 12 meters is about the length of two full-sized cars, a realistic distance to push a box in 3 seconds.
